q: Calcium carbonate is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which equation is correct?
explain: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Calcium forms Ca²⁺, so two Cl⁻ are needed and 2HCl balances the equation.

q: What is meant by an anhydrous substance?
options: a substance that absorbs water from air
a substance chemically combined with water
explain: Anhydrous means 'without water'.

q: A solution turns red litmus paper blue and turns thymolphthalein blue. What can be concluded?
options: The solution is a salt solution only.
explain: Both red litmus turning blue and thymolphthalein turning blue are positive tests for an alkali.

q: Which statement about the oxide of an element X is correct if the solution made by dissolving it in water turns litmus red?
options: X is probably a noble gas.
X must be a transition element.
explain: A non-metal oxide dissolving in water gives an acidic solution, which turns litmus red.

q: A student wants to prepare pure crystals of potassium nitrate. Which reagents should be used?
options: potassium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid
potassium hydroxide and dilute sulfuric acid
potassium hydroxide solution and dilute nitric acid
explain: Potassium is too reactive to add directly. The alkali and acid are mixed in exact amounts found by titration.

q: Which observation is expected when excess dilute sodium hydroxide is added to solid aluminium oxide with stirring?
explain: Because it is amphoteric, aluminium oxide reacts with the alkali and dissolves.

q: Which equation for the reaction of zinc oxide with sulfuric acid is correct?
explain: Zinc forms Zn²⁺, so the salt is ZnSO₄. The metal oxide acts as a base, giving a salt and water.

q: Solutions of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid have the same concentration of 0.1 mol/dm³. Which statement is correct?
options: Hydrochloric acid has the lower pH.
Ethanoic acid has the lower pH.
Ethanoic acid has the higher concentration of H⁺ ions.
explain: Hydrochloric acid is fully dissociated so it has more H⁺ ions per dm³ and a lower pH than the partly dissociated ethanoic acid.

q: A solution has a pH of 10. What is the colour of litmus in this solution?
explain: pH 10 is alkaline and litmus is blue in alkaline solutions.

q: Which substance acts as a proton acceptor in the equation NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺?
options: The H⁺ ion and NH₄⁺ ion together
explain: NH₃ gains an H⁺ ion, so it accepts a proton and is acting as a base.

q: Ammonia reacts with water: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. Which species acts as the proton donor in the forward reaction?
explain: Water donates an H⁺ ion to ammonia, which accepts it. The proton donor is the acid.

q: Which oxide reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to form a salt and water?
explain: A basic oxide neutralises an acid. CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O.

q: Which equation shows that hydrochloric acid is a strong acid?
explain: The single forward arrow shows complete dissociation into H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

q: A student adds magnesium ribbon to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which observation is correct?
options: The ribbon turns blue and no bubbles are seen.
The ribbon gets smaller and bubbles are seen.
A white precipitate forms at once.
The solution turns red and the ribbon grows.
explain: Magnesium reacts with the acid, dissolving and releasing bubbles of hydrogen gas.

q: What is meant by a strong acid?
options: an acid with a high concentration
an acid that reacts only with metals
an acid that is partially dissociated in aqueous solution
an acid that is completely dissociated in aqueous solution
explain: Strength describes the extent of dissociation, not concentration. A strong acid dissociates fully into ions.

q: What is meant by water of crystallisation?
options: water used to dissolve a solid before crystallising
water left on the crystals after filtering
water molecules that are part of the structure of hydrated crystals
water formed when an acid reacts with a base
explain: Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules chemically combined within the crystals.

q: Which acid and base are used to prepare copper(II) sulfate crystals from copper(II) oxide?
options: dilute sulfuric acid and excess copper(II) oxide
dilute hydrochloric acid and excess copper(II) oxide
dilute sulfuric acid and excess copper
dilute nitric acid and excess copper(II) oxide
explain: The salt contains sulfate, so sulfuric acid is needed. Copper(II) oxide is an insoluble base that can be added in excess.

q: Pink cobalt(II) chloride crystals, CoCl₂•6H₂O, are heated. Which colour change occurs?
explain: Hydrated cobalt(II) chloride is pink. When heated it loses water and turns blue.

q: Which statement about the oxides of period 3 elements and their character is correct?
options: Aluminium oxide shows both acidic and basic properties.
explain: Al₂O₃ is amphoteric, sodium oxide is basic and sulfur dioxide is acidic.

q: Which pair of aqueous solutions could be used to make lead(II) sulfate?
explain: Pb²⁺ with SO₄²⁻ gives insoluble lead(II) sulfate; the sodium nitrate formed is soluble and stays in the filtrate.

q: Calcium oxide is added to water and the solution is tested with red litmus paper. What is observed?
explain: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ forms an alkaline solution, which turns red litmus blue.

q: Why can lead(II) nitrate not be made by adding excess lead to dilute nitric acid?
options: Lead is too unreactive to react well with dilute acid.
explain: Lead reacts only very slowly with dilute acids. Lead(II) oxide or carbonate is usually used instead.

q: Which compound is formed when excess zinc carbonate is added to dilute sulfuric acid?
explain: ZnCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂.

q: A 25.0 cm³ sample of aqueous sodium hydroxide of concentration 0.100 mol/dm³ is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid. What is the concentration of the acid?
explain: Moles NaOH = 0.0250 × 0.100 = 0.00250 mol. NaOH and HCl react 1:1, so the concentration of HCl = 0.00250 ÷ 0.0200 = 0.125 mol/dm³.

q: Which solution would turn universal indicator paper purple?
explain: Strongly alkaline solutions of about pH 13 turn universal indicator purple.

q: Which ions are always present in aqueous solutions of alkalis?
explain: Alkalis produce hydroxide ions, OH⁻(aq), in water. Not all alkalis contain Na⁺.

q: What is the colour of litmus in dilute hydrochloric acid?
explain: Litmus is red in acidic solutions and blue in alkaline solutions.

q: What is the formula of hydrated copper(II) sulfate?
explain: Hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals contain five molecules of water per formula unit.

q: A salt solution is cooled and crystals form. What should be done to dry the crystals?
options: Pat them dry between filter paper.
Heat them strongly in a crucible.
explain: Gentle drying keeps the water of crystallisation; strong heating would drive it off.

q: Ammonium nitrate is warmed with calcium hydroxide. The gas produced turns damp red litmus paper blue. Which gas is it?
explain: Ammonia is the only common alkaline gas, so it turns damp red litmus blue. It is displaced from ammonium salts by bases.
